subject: Bio
title: Reproduction, ecology & human impact
sub: Plants and humans, organisms and the environment, human influences, conservation
strategyIntro: Cambridge Core Biology is assessed on Paper 1 (40 multiple-choice questions, 45 min), Paper 3 (structured theory questions, 1h 15, 80 marks) and Paper 6 (questions on experiments). Your school test may be shorter, but it will be marked the same way.

strategy.title: Multiple choice
points: About a minute per question. If one is taking longer, mark it and move on.
Cross out options you know are wrong first. Two often look similar: read every word.
Never leave one blank. A wrong answer loses nothing.

strategy.title: Structured questions
points: Marks go to keywords. Write the textbook term: “oviduct”, not “tube”.
The marks in brackets tell you how many separate points to make.
Label diagrams with a ruler line that touches the exact part.

strategy.title: Questions on experiments
points: Results tables: units go in the column headings, not next to each number.
Graphs: label both axes with units, choose an even scale, plot with small crosses.
Know the control variables and one safety precaution for each experiment.

strategy.title: Easy marks people lose
points: Writing “energy is made”. Energy is released, transferred or lost, never made.
Mixing up pollination (pollen moves) and fertilisation (nuclei fuse).
Saying the placenta “mixes blood”. Mother’s and baby’s blood never mix.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
quizIntro: Answer in Paper 1 style: about a minute each, eliminating wrong options first. Read the explanation after every answer, even when you get it right.

quiz.q: Which part of a flower produces pollen grains?
quiz.why: The anther (part of the stamen) makes pollen. The stigma receives it.

quiz.q: What is pollination?
options: Fusion of the nuclei of two gametes
Transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma
Spreading of seeds away from the parent plant
quiz.why: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. Fusion of nuclei is fertilisation.

quiz.q: Which is a feature of a wind-pollinated flower?
options: Feathery stigmas hanging outside the flower
quiz.why: Feathery stigmas outside the flower catch pollen from the air. The other three attract insects.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT needed for a seed to germinate?
quiz.why: Seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Many germinate underground in the dark.

quiz.q: Offspring produced by asexual reproduction are:
quiz.why: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no gametes, so offspring are genetically identical.

quiz.q: Where does fertilisation normally take place in humans?
quiz.why: The sperm meets the egg in the oviduct. The zygote then moves to the uterus to implant.

quiz.q: Which feature helps a sperm cell swim to the egg?
quiz.why: The flagellum (tail) moves the sperm. Its many mitochondria release energy for swimming.

quiz.q: Compared with a sperm cell, an egg cell is:
quiz.why: Egg cells are much larger and carry energy stores for the early embryo. They have a jelly coat that changes after fertilisation.

quiz.q: What is the main function of the placenta?
options: Exchanging substances between the mother’s blood and the fetus’s blood
Mixing the blood of mother and fetus
quiz.why: Oxygen and nutrients pass to the fetus; carbon dioxide and urea pass to the mother. The two bloods do not mix. Amniotic fluid protects from bumps.

quiz.q: Which hormone causes the development of male secondary sexual characteristics at puberty?
quiz.why: Testosterone is made by the testes. Oestrogen, made by the ovaries, does this in girls.

quiz.q: What happens during menstruation?
options: An egg is released from the ovary
The lining of the uterus breaks down and is lost
quiz.why: Menstruation is the loss of the uterus lining. Releasing an egg is ovulation, around the middle of the cycle.

quiz.q: HIV can be passed on by:
quiz.why: HIV spreads through body fluids: unprotected sex, shared needles, infected blood, and from mother to baby.

quiz.q: In a food chain, the arrows show:
options: Who eats whom, pointing at the eater’s prey
quiz.why: Arrows point from the organism eaten to the organism eating it: the direction energy moves.

quiz.q: Why are food chains usually no longer than five trophic levels?
options: Animals at the top are too large
Energy is lost at each level, so too little is left
quiz.why: Energy is lost at each level through respiration (heat), movement, and parts not eaten or not digested.

quiz.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
quiz.why: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide. The other three release it.

quiz.q: In eutrophication, why do fish die?
options: Decomposers use up the oxygen in the water
quiz.why: Dead algae and plants are broken down by decomposers, which respire aerobically and use up the dissolved oxygen.

quiz.q: Which is a disadvantage of growing a crop as a monoculture?
quiz.why: One crop over a large area reduces biodiversity and lets pests spread fast, so more pesticide is used.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an effect of deforestation?
options: Increased carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
quiz.why: Deforestation reduces biodiversity. It also causes flooding and loss of soil.

quiz.q: A seed bank helps conservation by:
options: Storing seeds so species can be regrown if they become rare
quiz.why: Seed banks keep seeds of many species safe for years, so plants can be grown again and reintroduced.

quiz.q: Which factor would cause a population of rabbits to decrease?
quiz.why: Food supply, competition, predation and disease all affect how fast a population grows. Disease increases deaths.

flashIntro: These are close to Cambridge’s own wording. Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.back: A process resulting in genetically identical offspring from one parent.
Fusion of the nuclei of two gametes to form a zygote, producing offspring that are genetically different.
The fusion of the nuclei of gametes.
The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.
Pollen moves to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.
Pollen moves to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species.
A sex cell (sperm or egg in humans; pollen nucleus or ovule in plants).
The cell formed when two gamete nuclei fuse.
The start of growth of a seed into a seedling. Needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
Organ where substances pass between mother’s and fetus’s blood without the bloods mixing.
Fluid around the fetus that protects it from knocks.
An organism that makes its own organic nutrients, usually using energy from sunlight, by photosynthesis.
An organism that gets its energy by feeding on other organisms.
An organism that gets its energy from dead or waste organic material.
The position of an organism in a food chain or food web.
A group of organisms of one species living in the same area at the same time.
All the populations of different species in an ecosystem.
A community of organisms and their environment, interacting together.
Excess nutrients (e.g. nitrates) in water cause algae to grow, die and decompose, using up oxygen.
One produced as fast as it is removed from the environment, so it does not run out.

examIntro: Paper 3 style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme and give yourself one mark per point you made clearly. One point per mark is the rule.

exam.q: Explain how adding too much fertiliser to fields can lead to fish dying in a nearby lake.
points: Fertiliser (nitrate) is washed / leaches into the lake
Algae / water plants grow quickly
Algae block light, so plants below cannot photosynthesise and die
Algae and plants die
Decomposers (bacteria) increase and break down the dead material
Decomposers respire aerobically and use up dissolved oxygen
Fish cannot get enough oxygen for respiration and die
exam.note: Any 5. Keep them in order: examiners look for the sequence.

exam.q: State three ways an insect-pollinated flower is different from a wind-pollinated flower.
points: Large, brightly coloured petals (wind: small, dull or no petals)
Has nectar and / or scent (wind: none)
Anthers and stigma inside the flower (wind: hanging outside)
Stigma sticky (wind: feathery)
Pollen larger, sticky or spiky (wind: small, light, smooth, in large amounts)
exam.note: Any 3. Each point must say which flower it describes, or compare both.

exam.q: Describe the function of the placenta.
points: Oxygen passes from mother’s blood to fetus
Nutrients (glucose, amino acids) pass to the fetus
Carbon dioxide passes from fetus to mother
Urea / waste passes from fetus to mother
Acts as a barrier to some toxins and pathogens
exam.note: Any 3. Say which direction each substance moves.

exam.q: State the three conditions a seed needs to germinate.
points: Water
Oxygen
A suitable temperature
exam.note: Light is not needed. Writing it does not lose marks but wastes time.

exam.q: Explain why only a small part of the energy in grass ends up in a cow’s body tissues.
points: Not all the grass is eaten (e.g. roots)
Some is not digested and is lost in faeces
Energy is released in respiration and lost as heat
Energy is used for movement
Energy lost in excretion (urine)
exam.note: Any 3. Never say energy is “used up” on its own: say how it is lost.

exam.q: Describe the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle.
points: They break down dead organisms and waste
They respire, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere

exam.q: Suggest two reasons why scientists keep seeds of endangered plants in seed banks.
points: Seeds can be stored for a long time
Plants can be regrown and reintroduced if the species dies out in the wild
Keeps genetic variation / diversity for the future
Protects plants that may be useful as medicines or food

exam.q: Describe the differences between a sperm cell and an egg cell.
points: Sperm is much smaller than the egg
Sperm has a flagellum and can move; egg cannot move by itself
Egg has energy stores (cytoplasm); sperm has very little
Egg has a jelly coat
Sperm made in large numbers; eggs one a month
Sperm has an acrosome with enzymes / many mitochondria
exam.note: Any 3. Each point must mention both cells.
